summary: Extends the Sieve email filtering language so scripts can examine and change the MIME parts of a message. It adds ways to test parts, loop over them, extract text, and replace or enclose parts. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Email filters usually look at the outside of a letter. This extension lets them open the envelope and check each page inside, and even swap a page or put the whole letter inside another.

questions: how to filter mime parts with sieve
how does the sieve replace action work
subtitle: Sieve extensions that let mail filters look inside, loop over, replace and wrap the MIME parts of a message.

tldr.problem: The base Sieve email filtering language has no loops and cannot target individual MIME body parts, so filters cannot easily act on attachments or nested parts.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5703 adds a foreverypart loop with break, :mime and :anychild arguments for the header, address and exists tests, and the replace, enclose and extracttext actions.
tldr.outcome: Scripts can now test, extract, replace or wrap parts of a message. Changing content can break digital signatures, and the RFC lists this as a security concern.

today: RFC 5703 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends the base language in RFC 5228.

sections.title: Why Sieve Needs MIME Tools
sections.content:
MIME messages are often complex objects made of many parts and sub-parts. Sieve is the email filtering language defined in RFC 5228. RFC 5703 is an extension to it that adds ways to test MIME body parts, loop through them, extract information from one, change the contents of one, and enclose the whole message in a wrapper.

Each feature is a separate Sieve capability that a script must name in its require line: foreverypart, mime, replace, enclose and extracttext.
sections.eli5: A normal filter only reads the address on the envelope. This extension teaches it to look at every page inside.

sections.title: Looping with foreverypart and break
sections.content:
The base Sieve language has no looping. The new foreverypart command walks through every MIME part of a message, including nested parts, depth first. It runs the same block of commands on each part, which becomes the current context in turn.

The break command ends the loop early. Both take an optional :name, so a break can end a named enclosing loop. It is an error if no enclosing loop has that name.

Loops can be nested. An inner loop only visits the children of the part the outer loop is on, and it is ignored if that part has no children. Implementations MAY limit nesting depth, but MUST support at least one loop inside another.
sections.eli5: It is like going through a box of folders one by one, and stopping as soon as you find the one you wanted.

sections.title: MIME-Aware Tests
sections.content:
The existing header, address and exists tests gain two new arguments. :mime makes the test parse MIME header lines. :anychild may only be used together with :mime, and widens the test to descendant parts.

Where the test looks depends on context. Outside a loop without :anychild, it sees only the top-level message headers. Inside foreverypart, it sees the current part. With :anychild it checks all MIME parts, or the current part and everything nested under it, and is true if any of them matches.

The header test with :mime adds options to inspect structured headers: :type, :subtype, :contenttype and :param. For a Content-Type header, these test the MIME type, the subtype, or both combined. :param tests named parameters such as a filename. Implementations SHOULD decode parameter values encoded as in RFC 2231.

With the :count option from RFC 5231, the type options count headers that parsed successfully, and :param counts matching parameters found.
sections.eli5: The filter can now ask questions like "is this page a picture?" or "is any page in the whole stack a web page?"

sections.title: The replace Action
sections.content:
The replace action swaps a MIME part for text given in the command. Inside a foreverypart loop it replaces the current part. If that part is multipart, all its children go too, and the change takes effect at once, so the running loop does not enter the removed parts. Outside a loop it replaces the entire message.

Without :mime, the replacement is a text/plain part in UTF-8. With :mime, the string is a full MIME entity with headers and content.

When the whole message is replaced, :subject sets a new subject and :from sets a new From address. Implementations MUST keep the old values as Original-Subject and Original-From, and MUST keep all other headers except those about the replaced MIME structure. If :mime is given together with :subject or :from, those two MUST be ignored, which SHOULD be flagged as a compilation error.
sections.eli5: It is like cutting out one page of a letter and gluing in a note that says what was removed, while writing down who originally sent it.

sections.title: The enclose Action
sections.content:
The enclose action wraps the entire message as an attachment to a new message. The original becomes a multipart/mixed message with two parts: a text/plain part holding the string argument, and a message/rfc822 part holding the original.

The optional :subject sets the subject, otherwise it comes from the enclosed message. Headers named in :headers are copied from the old message. If not specified, Date and From should be synthesized from the current date and the user running the action.

Later actions and tests work on the new message, so replace and similar actions should run before enclose. Several enclose actions enclose the message several times. The action does not affect messages sent with redirect.
sections.eli5: It puts the whole letter inside a new envelope, with a note on top explaining why.

sections.title: The extracttext Action
sections.content:
The extracttext action copies text from the current MIME part into a variable, as defined in RFC 5229. It is meant for use inside foreverypart. Servers MUST be able to transcode any textual part to UTF-8, which means undoing the transfer encoding and converting the character set.

The :first number limits how many characters are stored. Without it, the whole part is stored, though an implementation MAY truncate to its own limits. If the encoding or charset is unrecognized or invalid, the result is an empty string. Used outside a loop it sets the variable to an empty string, which SHOULD be a compilation error. To be useful it also needs the variables and foreverypart capabilities.
sections.eli5: It copies the first few words from a page onto a sticky note so the filter can use them later.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives three scripts. The first uses foreverypart and replace to strip some Windows executable attachments, matching on a application/exe content type or a filename ending in .com. The second finds attachments with executable-looking filename extensions and uses enclose to wrap the message with a warning. The third pulls the first 100 characters of the first text part out of a message from the boss, then breaks out of the loop.

The RFC says the lists of executable types in these examples are only samples, since the real list is considerably longer and constantly changing.
sections.eli5: The examples show filters that remove risky attachments, add a warning, or grab the first few words of a message.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because enclose creates a whole new message, site policies for message submission should be enforced. When it wraps a message containing a multipart/signed part, the original MUST be copied octet-for-octet so the signature stays valid.

Any change to message content can interfere with digital signatures. In particular, replace changes body content and so affects the body hash in DKIM signatures, and the signatures used by S/MIME, PGP and OpenPGP. The RFC also notes that the MIME structure of decrypted content in a multipart/encrypted part cannot be examined.

Systems MUST be sized and restricted so that even malicious MIME part matching does not deny service to other users of the host. The security considerations of base Sieve also apply.
sections.eli5: If you change a sealed letter, the seal no longer matches. So be careful when a filter edits mail that was signed.
